hints.title: Simultaneous Cell Transition Obstacle
hints.text: Updating cell states directly overwrites current values needed by adjacent neighbor calculations in the same generation. How can encoding past and next states into integer bit representations preserve history in place?

hints.title: Two-Bit State Transition Invariant
hints.text: Represent states using two bits: bit 0 is the current state, bit 1 is the next state. A transition from 0 to 1 becomes 2 (0b10), and from 1 to 1 becomes 3 (0b11).

hints.title: In-Place Bit Encoding Procedure
hints.text: For every cell (r, c), count active neighbors by checking bit 0: (board[nr][nc] & 1). Apply Conway rules: live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbors sets bit 1 (board[r][c] |= 2). Dead cell with 3 live neighbors sets bit 1 (board[r][c] |= 2). In a second pass, right-shift every cell by 1: board[r][c] >>= 1.

hints.title: Complete Implementation

complexity.notes: Every cell checks its 8 neighbors in O(1) time and encodes new state in place.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Cloning the board takes O(M * N) auxiliary memory.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Two-bit encoding eliminates auxiliary grid allocation entirely.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Using bit manipulation or state codes (-1, 2) to store past and future states in place.
